title: Inference operator debt mitigation strategies
body:
TL;DR:
This is a practical, sales-and-product-facing brief that reframes self-hosted inference from a technology comparison (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM) into an operator-debt and risk management conversation.

Goal:
- Give field teams concise, differentiated messaging vs common open stacks.
- Surface real hidden costs and failure modes for engineers evaluating a self-hosted route.
- Provide a lightweight runbook (what customer faces at weeks 1, 4, 12) and mitigations.

Audience:
- Platform/ML infra leads considering run vs rent for LLM serving.
- Head of ML/CTO at mid-market to enterprise.
- Solutions engineers prepping demos and POCs.

Quick stack snapshot (what buyers mean when they say the names):
- vLLM (open-serving-focused): fast start, great for research and low-latency prototypes. Weak spot: production autoscaling, multi-tenant isolation, memory fragmentation on long-lived KV caches.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference): more polished integrations (HF/transformers) and model format compatibility; often used as a higher-level orchestration on top of custom kernels. Weak spot: not tailored for heavy batching and cost/density tradeoffs across GPU types.
- TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA optimized): extreme performance for supported models and hardware; weak spot: portability, model compatibility, and operational drain when models or sequence lengths vary.

Operator-debt taxonomy (short list of hidden burdens we see in the field):
1) Fragmented kernel/format chasing: teams spend weeks matching model-export artifacts to runtime kernels.
2) Eviction cascades from KV/cache misconfig: small changes in prompt lengths cause huge memory pressure and OOMs.
3) Unpredictable tail latency under mixed workloads: batching policies tuned for avg latency fail with mixed short/long sequences.
4) Upgrade & rollback cost: lack of safe rollout primitives (canary, instant fallback) = long maintenance windows and manual rollbacks.
5) GPU utilization vs availability tradeoffs: teams either overprovision (wasteful) or underprovision (SLO misses) without good autoscaling and routing.
6) Security & compliance gaps: private deployments end up wiring a nave control plane and missing auditing/KMS integration.

Failure-mode runbook (typical timeline and seller playbook):
- Week 0-2: Build optimism. Buyers prototype with a small cluster, see fast throughput numbers on bench models. Seller action: acknowledge and praise the fast start, introduce next-phase checklist (safeguards).
- Week 3-6: Surface pain. Memory leaks, OOMs, or burst-latency tail. Customers contact infra teams. Seller action: pivot messaging to operational cost, propose Redwood Dedicated trial or controlled migration path.
- Week 6-12: Ops sprawl. Multiple home-grown scripts, forked kernel patches, and manual rollouts. Seller action: show playbooks for rollouts, A/B traffic routing, and cost projections that include operator hours.
- Week 12+: Decision trigger. Either the customer invests heavily in internal platform (high TCO) or looks for a managed alternative. Seller action: package commitments and migration lanes (e.g., staged model pinning and shadow routing).

GTM messaging frames (short soundbites for calls/emails):
- "Fast to prototype, fragile at scale": acknowledge technical merits of open tooling, then focus on predictable SLOs and operator load.
- "Minimize operator debt, not just cloud spend": highlight hidden human costs and the cost of interruptions.
- "Control plane you can trust": compliance and safe rollouts reduce business risk, not just latency.

Battlecard: vLLM
- Strengths to concede: quick local dev loop, wide community, good for research.
- Real risk to emphasize: lacks battle-tested multi-tenant routing, automated fallback to cheaper model variants, and integrated prefix/KV caching that persists across restarts.
- Redwood counter bullets: we provide policy-driven routing, transparent token-level cost attribution, and KV caching that survives pod restarts and keeps latency SLOs.

Battlecard: TGI
- Strengths to concede: smoother HF model compatibility and conversion paths.
- Real risk to emphasize: orchestration alone does not fix quantization/precision regressions across GPUs or runtime-level tail-latency spikes under mixed workloads.
- Redwood counter bullets: validated quantization profiles, per-model performance profiles, and automatic kernel selection to avoid silent regressions.

Battlecard: TensorRT-LLM
- Strengths to concede: excellent throughput for supported models on NVIDIA fleet.
- Real risk to emphasize: vendor lock-in to NVIDIA HW tuning, brittle across model/sequence changes, heavy ops overhead when model format changes.
- Redwood counter bullets: multi-variant routing (you can fall back to cheaper CPU/quantized variants), hardware-agnostic performance baseline, and build-in canary/rollback.

Economics quick model (talk track for AE/SE):
- Conservative assumptions: 3 nodes prod cluster, 1 node staging, 2 dedicated SRE FTEs split across infra; internal infra ops ~0.4 FTE ongoing + 0.3 FTE for incident response during growth spikes.
- Hidden line-items to call out in pitch: patching/gen2 kernel work, tuning for new models, cross-team incident time, compliance audit prep.
- Comparative talktrack: initial infra capex seems low but 12-18 month NRE and 2x in-year ops are common—frame Redwood as shifting that recurring burden to a productized SLA.

Buyer personas and hooks:
- Platform Lead (primary): cares about autonomy and predictable latency. Hook: "We'll let you keep control over routing policies while removing the 1-2 FTE ops tax."
- Head of ML/CTO (economic): cares about unit cost & time to market. Hook: "Same API, 40-60% fewer infra incidents historically vs self-hosted clusters in our bench."
- Security/Compliance: cares about auditability and KMS. Hook: "Pre-integrated KMS options and audit logs tied to every request."

Objection handling (short scripts):
- "We can build this ourselves": "Sure—teams who build get velocity early but often add 1–2 platform engineers within 6 months for steady-state. We can show anonymized post-mortems where internal projects stalled for months on kernel/eviction issues."
- "TensorRT gives better perf": "For narrow model+hardware combinations yes. But most product teams change models frequently; our multivariant routing preserves perf while avoiding lock-in for future models."

Tactical SE playbook for POCs:
- Phase 0 (2 days): baseline latency/throughput on canonical model (customer picks one). Use our hosted endpoint to get a realistic performance/cost baseline.
- Phase 1 (1 week): deploy a small private cluster but mirror production traffic in shadow. Goal: observe tail-latency and KV/cache behavior.
- Phase 2 (2-4 weeks): add canary routing to Redwood for 10% traffic. Measure operational overhead and incidents. Use findings to produce a realistic 12-month TCO.

Win themes and experimental plays to try on target accounts:
- "Operator rescue" offering: short-term enticement to take over ops for first 90 days post-migration with bundled workshops and runbook handover.
- "Model change warranty": promise to manage regressions after a model change for 30 days post-rollout; shifts risk.
- Free quantization assessment: run a non-invasive audit that shows cost/perf tradeoffs across quantization levels; makes tradeoffs explicit.

Appendix: practical checklist for customer conversations (SEs)
- Ask what "success" looks like at 3 months and 12 months (SLOs, cost targets, ops headcount).
- Validate: how many model changes per month; typical prompt length distribution; burstiness profile.
- Probe: incident history—downtime, root causes, frequency.
- Show: token-level cost attribution example + operator hours estimate.

Appendix B: short eval rubric we give customers (one-pager)
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for short (<64 tok) and long (>512 tok).
- Stability: number of major incidents per 30 days; mean time to recovery (MTTR) when load increases.
- Operational overhead: calendar hours per week spent maintaining runtime/config/tuning.
- Portability: time to move a model from dev to prod in hours.

Notes & follow-ups:
- Next action: craft a short one-pager for AEs that maps the above to a single-page slide they can put in outreach.
- Experiment proposal: run 6 closed POCs targeting mid-market platform teams with the "operator rescue" bundle and measure win rate.

Unresolved questions to answer in product & bench teams:
- Empirical: median operator load (hours/week) across customers who attempted self-hosted then migrated. (Dev -> bench ask).
- Product: what are the minimum rollback latency metrics we need to market as a differentiator (seconds/minutes?).
- Legal: what compliance artifacts are most requested by regulated customers when evaluating private deployments?

References and internal links (examples):
- Internal incident postmortems (redacted) showing eviction cascade case studies.
- Draft of quantization audit tool in GH (linked above).

Author notes (why this doc is different):
This is deliberately operator-first rather than pure tech-performance. The existing corpus covers many build-vs-buy and technical battlegrounds; this doc reframes the conversation around ongoing human and risk costs, and gives the field a concrete week-by-week runbook and POC plan to use in the wild.

END
